concepts_taught: horizontal and vertical projectile motions are independent but share time
horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is g downward when air resistance is negligible
an initial angled velocity can be resolved into perpendicular components
constant horizontal motion combined with constant vertical acceleration produces a parabolic path
vertical motion determines projectile flight time
the shared flight time gives horizontal range
impact velocity is the vector sum of final horizontal and vertical components
skills_students_can_now_use: resolve an initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components
state the velocity and acceleration properties of each projectile component
sketch and explain an ideal parabolic projectile path
calculate projectile flight time from vertical motion
calculate horizontal range using the shared time
calculate final vertical velocity with signed data
determine impact speed and direction from perpendicular components
analyse angled projectiles with unequal launch and landing levels
next_module_can_assume: students can separate horizontal and vertical projectile motion
students can complete ideal projectile calculations for time, range and impact velocity
students can select and apply component equations in a mixed kinematics problem
students can state a resultant velocity magnitude and direction
next_module_must_not_assume: students can optimise range with launch angle
students have studied later-topic forces or energy unless supplied
